new_statements.quote: Hup also has two contrastive tones, realized on stressed syllables [p. 450] […] The canonical (and minimal, as noted below) monomorphemic prosodic word is a single CVC syllable with one stress/tone locus; e.g. mɔ̌y ‘house’. […] Again, there is only one stress/tone locus, which occurs almost without exception on the second syllable. [p. 470] […] In verbs, as noted above, multimorphemic strings maximally take between one and two primary stress/tone loci. These normally occur on the boundary suffix and/or on the preceding syllable [p. 473]

Tallman, Sandra Auderset & Hiroto Uchihara (eds.), Constituency and convergence in the Americas, 447-482. Berlin: Language Science Press. new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (820 pp., text layer present; pdfinfo title 'Constituency and convergence in the Americas', LangSci 291) and its. All four quoted fragments are present verbatim at the stated locators: 'Hup also has two contrastive tones, realized on stressed syllables' sits in the §2 overview paragraph immediately before the printed page number 450 (the same paragraph lists the 9 vowels and 19 consonants and footnote 2 defines the tone diacritics: acute = high tone or its falling allophone, hacek = rising tone); §5.1 'Overview: Concentric phonological domains' item (a) 'The canonical (and minimal, as noted below) monomorphemic prosodic word is a single CVC syllable with one stress/tone loc…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Hup is a word-accent (tonal-accent) language: a high (with falling allophone) or rising tone is realised on the stressed syllable. Roots are canonically one CVC syllable carrying the single stress/tone locus; the rare bisyllabic and reduplicated roots stress the second (final) syllable. In inflected verbs there are one or two primary stress/tone loci, normally on the obligatory boundary suffix and/or the syllable before it, the choice being lexically fixed by that suffix; in noun phrases stress is culminative over the whole phrase (demonstrative+noun, noun+adjective take one primary stress) and its locus depends on the identity of roots, adjectives, classifiers and suffixes. So stress is right-edge oriented but morphologically determined rather than counted from the word edge.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; the source speaks only of 'one or two primary stress/tone loci' per domain (verb complex or noun phrase) and of certain nominal suffixes 'lexically marked to receive an additional stress' (p. 474).
new_statements.exceptions: The 'filler' suffix -Vw and the inchoative -ay never receive stress/tone (p. 473); enclitics are unstressed CVC morphemes whereas particles (after position 26) receive independent stress/tone (pp. 460, 473); pre-verbal pronominal subjects are unstressed and in the Upper Rio Tiquié dialect reduced to tV- (p. 455); an incorporated simplex O between a valence-adjusting preformative and the verb is unstressed while the preformative then receives stress/tone (pp. 458, 473); 'one or two exceptional patterns' of locus placement, lexically determined by the boundary suffix (p. 471).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the prosodic/grammatical word rather than the phrase for verbs (stress/tone domain = verb-complex positions 2/3-26, i.e. root(s) through boundary suffix and enclitics) but the noun phrase for nouns (positions 5-15; one primary stress per NP). Examples are from Epps's naturalistic corpus and elicitation (Tiquié-river Hup, Brazil); the same conventions are stated to follow Epps 2008a, which is the fuller treatment. Ramirez 2006 (p. 33) independently confirms the two-tone (high vs rising) contrast but says nothing about stress placement.
new_statements.identity_note: The description is of Hup proper (hupd1244), Epps's corpus from the Tiquié-river communities in Brazil (dialects Tat Dëh, Barreira, Umari Norte, Nova Fundação); one dialect-specific note concerns Upper Rio Tiquié pronoun reduction. Giacone 1955 calls the language 'Ubde-Nehern ou Macú' and Moore & Franklin 'Makú-Hupda'; all the same language. Sister language Yuhup (yuhu1238) is treated separately in the literature (Lopes & Parker 1999) and was not used here.

sources.note: Tertiary, summarising Epps 2008: 'Hup tonality functions in what is called a word-accent system... the contrast is restricted to one syllable per word, which is predictable and also exhibits other features of stressed syllables (greater intensity, longer duration, and higher pitch)'; pt: 'tonicidade da palavra, que combina tom contrastivo e estresse lexical' (Epps 2008: 82-98).

sources.note: 'ACENTUAÇÃO', p. 33: 'A língua hup é tonal: ela permite diferenciar o sentido das palavras só pelo tipo de melodia tonal associada à(s) vogal(is)'; high tone written with acute, rising tone with grave; minimal pairs (moh 'lago' vs moh 'inambu'). No statement on stress placement; entry yup (p. 217) notes a following noun 'perde o tom dele'.

sources.citation: Giacone, Antônio. 1955. Pequena gramática e dicionário português ubde-nehern ou macú. Recife: Missão Indígena Salesiana / Escola Salesiana de Artes Gráficas. viii+103 pp.
sources.note: p. 9 'Sinais diacríticos': acute = 'acento tónico'; pp. 10-11: diminutive -me, genitive -ne and plural -de leave 'invariável o acento tónico da palavra'; p. 24: a verb's accent that is 'agudo' in the present becomes closed/nasalized in the past for some verbs. Missionary orthography, no placement rule; words are cited with the accent marked (e.g. Nhambó, Hammái, Bocdéu).
